title: Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)

teacherSummary.text: Polyneices asks his father's pardon and help in the war on Thebes. Oedipus curses him: the brothers will die by each other's hands. Antigone begs Polyneices to turn back; he refuses and asks his sisters to bury him if the curse comes true, which sets up Antigone.

anchorPassages.text:
Now, father, let me tell thee why I came.
I have been banished from my native land
Because by right of primogeniture
I claimed possession of thy sovereign throne
Wherefrom Eteocles, my younger brother,
Ousted me, not by weight of precedent,
Nor by the last arbitrament of war,
But by his popular acts; and the prime cause
Of this I deem the curse that rests on thee.
So likewise hold the soothsayers, for when
I came to Argos in the Dorian land
And took the king Adrastus’ child to wife,
Under my standard I enlisted all
The foremost captains of the Apian isle,
To levy with their aid that sevenfold host
Of spearmen against Thebes, determining
To oust my foes or die in a just cause.
Why then, thou askest, am I here today?
Father, I come a suppliant to thee
Both for myself and my allies who now
With squadrons seven beneath their seven spears
Beleaguer all the plain that circles Thebes.

anchorPassages.text:
O villain, when thou hadst the sovereignty
That now thy brother holdeth in thy stead,
Didst thou not drive me, thine own father, out,
An exile, cityless, and make me wear
This beggar’s garb thou weepest to behold,
Now thou art come thyself to my sad plight?
Nothing is here for tears; it must be borne
By me till death, and I shall think of thee
As of my murderer; thou didst thrust me out;
’Tis thou hast made me conversant with woe,
Through thee I beg my bread in a strange land;
And had not these my daughters tended me
I had been dead for aught of aid from thee.
They tend me, they preserve me, they are men
Not women in true service to their sire;
But ye are bastards, and no sons of mine.

anchorPassages.note: Paternal curse seals mutual slaughter and bridges toward Antigone.
anchorPassages.text:
That city thou canst never storm, but first
Shalt fall, thou and thy brother, blood-imbrued.
Such curse I lately launched against you twain,
Such curse I now invoke to fight for me,
That ye may learn to honour those who bare thee
Nor flout a sightless father who begat
Degenerate sons—these maidens did not so.
Therefore my curse is stronger than thy “throne,”
Thy “suppliance,” if by right of laws eterne
Primeval Justice sits enthroned with Zeus.
Begone, abhorred, disowned, no son of mine,
Thou vilest of the vile! and take with thee
This curse I leave thee as my last bequest:—
Never to win by arms thy native land,
No, nor return to Argos in the Vale,
But by a kinsman’s hand to die and slay
Him who expelled thee. So I pray and call
On the ancestral gloom of Tartarus
To snatch thee hence, on these dread goddesses
I call, and Ares who incensed you both
To mortal enmity. Go now proclaim
What thou hast heard to the Cadmeians all,
Thy staunch confederates—this the heritage
That Oedipus divideth to his sons.

My sisters, ye his daughters, ye have heard
The prayers of our stern father, if his curse
Should come to pass and ye some day return
To Thebes, O then disown me not, I pray,
But grant me burial and due funeral rites.
So shall the praise your filial care now wins
Be doubled for the service wrought for me.

objective: Students will analyze how conflict develops in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” by writing a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph that cites at least 2 quotations from the section, and will score at least 80% on the section quiz.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.text: What does Polyneices promise his father if the war at Thebes succeeds?
items.lookFor: To establish him at home again. After asking pardon and aid, he offers this return as the reward of victory, a promise spoken in the plea, not a report that the city has already been taken.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: To establish him at home again. After asking pardon and aid, he offers this return as the reward of victory, a promise spoken in the plea, not a report that the city has already been taken.

items.text: Why is Polyneices' plea for mercy unsuccessful?
items.lookFor: His father cannot forgive his abandonment; the curse is already set. Polyneices also asks for help in a war against his own city, so his plea for mercy is bound to a request for an ally.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Polyneices admits, “I own it, and am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee” (lines 1322–1323), but his plea is tied to a war: he wants his father’s favour because “victory, if oracles speak true, / Will fall to those who have thee for ally” (lines 1386–1387). Oedipus hears a son who came only when he needed him, and answers with the curse he “lately launched against you twain” (line 1428).

items.text: What does “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” suggest about Polyneices and the father's curse? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: The curse makes a family’s past its future: the father’s curse decides how the sons will die, and Polyneices’ burial request is the seed of Antigone.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The scene suggests that a family’s past wrongs shape its future. Oedipus curses his son “by a kinsman’s hand to die and slay / Him who expelled thee” (lines 1441–1442), and Polyneices goes knowingly toward that end, asking his sisters, “grant me burial and due funeral rites” (line 1461). A request made in this scene reaches beyond the play into the sisters’ future.

items.text: Find one example of conflict in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”. What does it reveal about Polyneices and the father's curse that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: A specific clash, such as Antigone’s attempt to turn her brother back, explained for what it reveals: Polyneices chooses ruin rather than shame, so the curse works through his own choice.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Antigone begs, “Turn back thy host to Argos with all speed, / And ruin not thyself and Thebes as well” (lines 1466–1467), and he answers, “’Tis shame to live in exile” (line 1472). The clash shows that the curse works through his own pride: he hears the prophecy and still says, “but I must not yield” (line 1476). A plain statement that he is cursed would miss that he walks into it.

items.text: How does the characterization in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” shape what we understand about Polyneices and the father's curse?
items.lookFor: How Polyneices is drawn as both sincere and self-serving (tears and confession, then a request for an ally), and Oedipus as justly wronged but terrible in anger, so neither is simply right.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Polyneices weeps and confesses, “I scorn myself” (line 1323), yet his speech quickly becomes a recruiting appeal for a war on his own city (lines 1365–1387). Oedipus has a real grievance, “Didst thou not drive me, thine own father, out” (line 1408), but answers with a terrible curse. Neither is drawn as simply right, so the audience has to weigh a son’s late remorse against a father’s justified anger.

items.text: In the passage that opens with “Ah me, my sisters…”, why might Sophocles have chosen these particular words? Pick two and explain their connotations.
items.lookFor: Two words from the opening of Polyneices’ speech (lines 1313–1323) with their connotations, such as “castaway,” “antic tatters,” “too late” or “vile,” showing pity, shame and self-accusation.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Polyneices calls his father “a castaway” (line 1315) clothed in “antic tatters” (line 1317). The words picture a shipwrecked man in ragged clothes, a shocking sight for a former king. Then he says, “All this too late I learn” (line 1321), which admits his neglect. The diction mixes pity with shame, which is what makes his plea sound sincere.

items.text: What causes the main turn in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”, and what effect is it likely to have on what follows?
items.lookFor: The turn is Oedipus breaking his silence, for Theseus’s sake, with a curse instead of a reply; the effect is that Polyneices goes to a war he now believes he will lose.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: The turn comes when Oedipus breaks his silence, “for Theseus’ sake / Who sent him hither” (lines 1401–1402), with “An answer that will bring him little joy” (line 1405), and then lays his curse on his son. The likely effect follows at once: Polyneices leaves knowing his march leads “to ruin” (line 1484), but he refuses to turn back.

items.text: How does “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” build on “Stasimon 3 (lines 1270–1307)”? Name one link of cause and effect.
items.lookFor: A cause-and-effect link: the ode’s list of strife and war, and the old man buffeted on every side, are given a face here in a son who wants his blind father’s help for a war against his own city.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Stasimon 3 named “Envy, sedition, strife, / Carnage and war” (lines 1292–1293) as the tale of life. Episode 4 makes that list concrete: Polyneices comes from a war of brothers, with an army that will “Beleaguer all the plain that circles Thebes” (line 1368). The ode’s gloom prepares the audience for a scene in which family strife becomes open war.

items.text: In “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”, what can we infer about a character's motives from what they say on stage about Polyneices and the father's curse, as opposed to what they claim?
items.lookFor: Polyneices claims to come in sorrow and pity, but his motive is to recruit his father as an ally; even his promise to bring his father home serves his own claim to the throne.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Polyneices claims pity for his father, but his own words reveal the motive: “victory, if oracles speak true, / Will fall to those who have thee for ally” (lines 1386–1387). Even his offer, “And bring thee home again and stablish thee, / And stablish, having cast him out, myself” (lines 1395–1396), ends with his own throne. His remorse may be real, but it comes when he needs something.

items.text: Go back to the bell-ringer question (Why do people refuse to turn back from a course they expect to fail?). Now that we have read closely, how would you revise your first answer, and which line changed your mind?
items.lookFor: A revised answer to the bell-ringer (why people refuse to turn back from a course they expect to fail), using Polyneices’ appeal to shame and his reasoning about leadership.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: I first said people are stubborn. Polyneices gives more specific reasons. One is shame: “’Tis shame to live in exile” (line 1472). The other is his position as a leader: “How could I lead again / An army that had seen their leader quail?” (lines 1468–1469). People keep going when turning back would cost them their pride and their place.

items.text: Where does foreshadowing appear in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”, and how does it connect Polyneices and the father's curse to the larger concern with law against force?
items.lookFor: Where foreshadowing appears (the curse on the brothers, the burial request) and how it connects to law against force: Polyneices brings force against his city, and Oedipus answers with a curse grounded in “laws eterne.”
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Oedipus foretells, “That city thou canst never storm, but first / Shalt fall, thou and thy brother, blood-imbrued” (lines 1426–1427), and Polyneices’ plea for burial (line 1461) points beyond the play. This connects to law against force: Polyneices brings armed force against his own city, and Oedipus answers by appealing to “laws eterne” (line 1434) and “Primeval Justice” (line 1435), claiming his curse is stronger than force.

items.text: Is Oedipus just or cruel to Polyneices? Defend your view with evidence.
items.lookFor: An evaluation with evidence for justice (the son’s neglect; the daughters’ care) and cruelty (a curse of mutual killing on his sons), weighed to a position, with a counterpoint.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: just in grievance, cruel in punishment. The grievance is real: “thou didst thrust me out” (line 1414), and “had not these my daughters tended me / I had been dead” (lines 1417–1418). But the curse, that both sons fall “blood-imbrued” (line 1427), goes far beyond answering one son’s neglect. Counter-line: Oedipus claims he only names what “just Heaven” already watches (line 1422), so the punishment may not be his alone.

items.text: Consider this reading of the scene (a claim, not a line from the text): The curse makes a family's past its future. Polyneices' burial request is the seed of Antigone. How far do you agree? Take a stand and defend it with two lines from the scene.
items.lookFor: A stand with two lines from the scene: the curse turns the family’s past into its future, and the burial request reaches beyond the play; a qualification that Polyneices also chooses his path.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: agree, with a qualification. The curse lays the past on the future: “by a kinsman’s hand to die and slay / Him who expelled thee” (lines 1441–1442), and the burial request, “grant me burial and due funeral rites” (line 1461), points beyond the play. But Polyneices also chooses: “The road I choose” (line 1482). The past shapes his future only because he refuses to turn back.

items.text: Which character in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” acts most wisely in the matter of Polyneices and the father's curse, and which least? Judge them by a standard you name.
items.lookFor: A named standard applied to two characters, for example care for the whole family: Antigone tries to save her brother and Thebes, while Polyneices chooses pride. Give a line for each.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: by the standard of care for the whole family, Antigone acts most wisely, pleading, “ruin not thyself and Thebes as well” (line 1467) and asking “What profit from thy country’s ruin comes?” (line 1471). By the same standard Polyneices acts least wisely, admitting that the road he chooses “Leads me to ruin” (line 1484). A student could choose Oedipus as least wise instead, for answering remorse with a curse on both his sons.

items.text: You are directing “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”. Make two staging choices (a line delivery, a movement, a light or sound cue) and explain how each shapes the audience's view of Polyneices and the father's curse.
items.lookFor: Two staging choices tied to lines, such as Oedipus’s long silence while his son pleads, or the farewell between brother and sister, each with its effect.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: (1) Through “Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away” (line 1329), keep Oedipus turned away and utterly still while Polyneices moves around him trying to catch his face. The silence becomes the father’s first answer. (2) On “Ye ne’er shall see my living face again” (line 1488), let Polyneices take his sisters’ hands, then pull free and leave without looking back. The audience feels both his love and his doom.

items.text: Write your own questions about “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”: one recall, one “why/how”, and one “should/what if”. Trade with a partner and answer theirs.
items.lookFor: Three questions answerable from lines 1308–1501: one recall, one why/how and one should/what-if, different in kind.
followUps: Which of your questions was hardest to answer from the text, and why?
Which line did your partner use, and does it really answer your why/how question?
items.answerGuidance: Model set. Recall: Where does Polyneices say he has been living and gathering allies? (Argos, where he married the king’s daughter, lines 1357–1358.) Why/how: Why does Oedipus speak to his son at all? (Only for Theseus’s sake, lines 1401–1402.) Should/what if: Should Polyneices have told his allies about the curse? (He says a general “Reports successes and conceals mishaps,” line 1480; answers weigh honesty against his duty as a leader.)

items.text: Connect “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)”, with its focus on Polyneices and the father's curse, to death and blessing: is the link strong or weak so far? What would Sophocles need to show next to strengthen it?
items.lookFor: A judgment about death and blessing, the question’s theme. Oedipus can bless and curse with his death in view; here he curses his son, while his blessing is reserved for those who cared for him. A strong answer says what must come next.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: the link is strong but one-sided. In this scene Oedipus’s power is a curse, calling on “the ancestral gloom of Tartarus / To snatch thee hence” (lines 1443–1444), while Polyneices, facing death, can only pray that his sisters “may escape all ill” (line 1500). The blessing Oedipus promised Athens (lines 92–93) has not yet been shown. To strengthen the link, Sophocles must show how his death becomes a blessing for those who received him.

items.text: Is the conflict in “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” effective in presenting Polyneices and the father's curse, or does it feel heavy-handed? Evaluate it as a reader would in a review.
items.lookFor: A judgment against a stated criterion (is the conflict balanced, letting both sides speak?), with a line that meets it and one passage that might miss it.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: One defensible answer: effective, because both sides make real arguments. Polyneices admits his guilt (“I scorn myself,” line 1323), and Oedipus answers with a real grievance (lines 1406–1418). Counter-line: the long list of the seven captains (lines 1369–1381) may feel heavy-handed or slow to a modern audience. A reviewer could cut it, though it shows how large the war Polyneices brings really is.

items.text: Compare how “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” treats Polyneices and the father's curse with how another text, film or event you know treats a similar idea. What does Oedipus at Colonus see that the other misses?
items.lookFor: A named comparison (another story of a parent who refuses a child’s plea, or of brothers at war) and one thing the episode sees that the other misses, tied to a line.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Compare the parable of the prodigal son, where the father forgives at once. Episode 4 sees what happens when the child’s remorse comes with a demand and arrives too late: “All this too late I learn” (line 1321). It also shows a sister trying to stop the damage, “Turn back thy host to Argos” (line 1466). The play sees that forgiveness can fail, and that the cost then falls on the whole family.

items.text: Predict what “Thunder scene (lines 1502–1605)” will bring, using two clues from this scene. After reading, evaluate your prediction.
items.lookFor: A prediction from two clues, Oedipus’s promise from Phoebus that signs would mark his end and the scene’s turn toward death, about what the next scene will bring, checked after reading.
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: Clue 1: in the Prologue Oedipus said he was promised signs of his end, “Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash” (line 95). Clue 2: this scene is full of farewells and death, “Ye ne’er shall see my living face again” (line 1488). A reasonable prediction is that the promised sign will come and Oedipus will prepare for his own end, and perhaps send for Theseus. After reading, students check how the sign arrived.

items.text: Design a one-paragraph modern adaptation of “Episode 4 (lines 1308–1501)” (setting, characters, conflict). What must stay the same for it to still be about Polyneices and the father's curse?
items.lookFor: An adaptation that keeps the core: an estranged son comes to ask a wronged parent for support in a fight against his brother, is refused with a terrible judgment, and asks his sister for one last favour. It names two details that must stay.
followUps: Which line from the scene does your piece depend on? Read it to us.
What did you keep from the original, and what did you change on purpose?
items.answerGuidance: Model answer: A son who ignored his father for years arrives at the shelter where his sisters care for him, asking for his public endorsement in a ruinous lawsuit against his brother. The father refuses and disowns both sons, and the son asks his sister to stand by him if he loses everything. Two things must stay: the remorse that comes only with a request (lines 1386–1387), and the sister’s plea to turn back (lines 1466–1467).

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.
